title: The Scandal at 1612 Prairie
premise: A carriage manufacturer's showplace has become the most discussed house on the block: a society divorce, a judge's order, a violin in a disabled automobile, and a small boy caught in the middle of it all.

opening.text:
JAUNT: THE SCANDAL AT 1612 PRAIRIE. A Monday afternoon in November 1904, at the quiet northern end of Prairie Avenue.

Four stops along one short block. The house at 1612 has been a showplace for twenty years; this year it has become a battlefield. A husband has gone to court, a judge has awarded the house to the wife, and in November the husband stood up in open court and made accusations about her that the entire city has now read in the Tribune. The neighbors keep their curtains closed and their ears wide open.

Begin next door, where you can picture the house as it once was.

stops.text: 1608 Prairie, and beside it the large square house at 1612. Twenty years ago it belonged to a Studebaker, of the Studebaker Brothers carriage works, and it was the most brilliant house on the street. In February 1884 some two hundred guests arrived here from a family wedding, and "the large residence was brilliantly illuminated, and every room was elaborately decorated with smilax and cut flowers". A society column of 1887 remarked on the traffic: "Morning and night, a showy turnout is noticed before the squarely-built house, with the number 1612 over the portals". A carriage manufacturer's house ought to display the finest carriages at its door, and it did. Observe it now: no turnout waits at the curb this afternoon, and a maid next door watches it from her steps. Walk to the gate of 1612.

stage.caption: A maid at 1608 sweeps her steps while keeping a watchful eye on the house next door.

stops.text: 1612 Prairie. The Tribune has the story, and so does everyone else. Last May the husband, Charles E. Brown, filed for divorce. His wife Catherine is twenty-seven, "the daughter of Gen. Graves, a wealthy resident of Buffalo", and the grounds were "habitual drunkenness and statutory charges". Judge Tuley then granted Mrs. Brown possession of this house, where she, her husband and their son had lived, along with $200 a month in temporary alimony while the suit was pending. So the wife occupies the fortress and the husband stands outside it. Behind those windows live a woman the newspapers have made notorious and a small boy. The house will survive until it is demolished around 1960. Step next door and learn what the husband alleged in November.

stage.caption: A lady steps out onto the porch of 1612, glances up and down the street, and retreats inside before anyone can approach.

cast.name: Catherine G. Brown (no card in the town; an unnamed figure plays her)

stops.text: 1616 Prairie, the next house south, where the neighbors read the Tribune over their coffee. In November Mr. Brown returned to court and charged that his wife "had conducted herself in a disgraceful manner, had been habitually intoxicated, and had done many freakish things, such as playing a violin in a broken automobile while a man pushed the machine along a public highway, and dancing about the rear of their home clothed only in a nightrobe". He went further and named a man, "E. C. Edsall, an automobile salesman", with whom, the husband charged, she fled to an eastern summer resort and later to New York City. It is the most delicious scandal on Prairie Avenue in years, and two maids on these steps are savoring it. But a divorce never involves only two people. Look for the boy.

stage.caption: Two maids on the steps of 1616 share the newspaper and glance across at 1612.

stops.text: Across the street at 1613, look back at the west side of the block. The boy is Charles Edward Brown, the couple's only son, and he is the true prize in this contest. A nurse walks him along the sidewalk past his own front door; his mother holds the house, while his father wants it back, and wants him. The court has not yet ruled. In the newspapers he is merely a line at the end of each story, but on this walk he is the only person in the entire affair who has done nothing at all. The Tribune will report the conclusion in March 1905, and by then the house, the boy and the woman will each have gone separate ways.

stage.caption: A nurse walks a small boy along the far sidewalk past the door of 1612, and he pauses to gaze up at it.

cast.name: Charles Edward Brown, the son (no card in the town; an unnamed figure plays him)

Next door to the south, where the neighbors hold the morning's Tribune.
Across Prairie Avenue to look back at the west side of the block.

endings.text: The walk ends here. After a bitter struggle, early in 1905, the husband prevailed, winning the divorce, the house on Prairie Avenue and custody of the boy. On 8 March 1905 he sold the property to Charles Palmerston Anderson, the Episcopal bishop of Chicago. That same week the Tribune discovered Catherine Brown in a police cell, arrested at 3667 Wabash Avenue, where police said she had been living as Kittie Casey, and fined $85 for disorderly conduct. "I am penniless", she said. "I cannot pay the fine". From her cell she added, "It's all because a woman is jealous of me, I guess". The general's daughter from Buffalo had held 1612 Prairie for less than a year, and the newspapers that made her famous told only her husband's side.

keepsake.title: The 1612 Court Papers
keepsake.text: An interpretive card of the Brown divorce of 1904 and 1905 as the Tribune reported it; a reconstruction for this walk, not a historical artifact.

evidence.text: On 21 February 1884 about 200 of the intimate friends and relatives of the bride and groom were received at the residence of W. F. Studebaker, No. 1612 Prairie avenue, after the Studebaker-Innis wedding. 'The large residence was brilliantly illuminated, and every room was elaborately decorated with smilax and cut flowers.'
evidence.locator: Chicago Tribune, 22 February 1884, 'Wedding Bells', as transcribed.

evidence.text: Inter Ocean, 2 January 1887: 'Morning and night, a showy turnout is noticed before the squarely-built house, with the number 1612 over the portals.' Its owner was one of the Studebaker Brothers, the carriage makers.

The Scandal at 1612 Prairie: the day, Monday 21 November 1904, the hour and the order of the walk are this jaunt's framing, chosen because the stories meet on it (three days after Arthur Caton's death, a Monday of the Reading Class, before Kimball's death in December). No visit on that day is asserted.

The Scandal at 1612 Prairie: who is seen at each stop, where they stand, what they do and when are reconstructed. People with cards in the town play themselves; people the town has no card for (and the unnamed servants, callers and passers-by) are unnamed figures in period dress, and no likeness is claimed. No word anyone says is asserted.

Catherine G. Brown was the 'former wife of Charles E. Brown, 1612 Prairie avenue'. Mrs. Brown, who is 27 years old and the daughter of Gen. Graves, a wealthy resident of Buffalo, first attracted notoriety in May, 1904, when her husband filed a bill for divorce. By a court order issued by Judge Tuley Mrs. Brown was given possession of the residence, 1612 Prairie avenue, where she and her husband and their son had lived, and was granted temporary alimony amounting to $200 a month while the suit was pending. Habitual drunkenness and statutory charges were the grounds.
evidence.locator: Chicago Tribune, 11 March 1905, 'Story of Divorce Case', as transcribed.

evidence.text: Joseph Goodman Residence, 1612 S. Prairie Avenue: razed circa 1960.

In November Mr. Brown appeared in court and charged that his wife had conducted herself in a disgraceful manner, had been habitually intoxicated, and had done many freakish things, such as playing a violin in a broken automobile while a man pushed the machine along a public highway, and dancing about the rear of their home clothed only in a nightrobe.
evidence.locator: Chicago Tribune, 11 March 1905, 'Story of Divorce Case', as transcribed.

evidence.text: He also charged her with receiving the attentions of E. C. Edsall, an automobile salesman. With Edsall, the husband charged, Mrs. Brown ran away to an eastern summer resort and later to New York City.
After a bitter fight Mr. Brown was granted a divorce about six weeks before 11 March 1905, and given possession of the Prairie avenue property, and the custody of the one son, Charles Edward Brown.
evidence.locator: Chicago Tribune, 11 March 1905, the last paragraph, as transcribed.

evidence.text: In March 1905 Mrs. Catherine G. Brown was arrested at 3667 Wabash avenue, where she had been living under the name of Kittie Casey, according to the police, and fined $85 for disorderly conduct. 'I am penniless,' she said. 'I cannot pay the fine.' In her cell she said: 'It's all because a woman is jealous of me, I guess.' Justice Hurley called her 'a problem in humanity to me.'
On 8 March 1905 the lot at 1612 Prairie passed from Brown (printed 'Chas. S. Brown') to the Rt. Rev. Chas. Palmerston Anderson, bishop of the Protestant Episcopal church in the diocese of Chicago.
evidence.locator: Chicago Tribune, 14 March 1905, the transfer list, as transcribed.
